core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Pulmonary Tuberculosis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Management includes respiratory isolation and public-health notification according to local protocol, appropriate sputum testing and imaging, HIV counselling and testing, and contact tracing. Specialist-directed multidrug treatment is started when indicated after diagnostic assessment and drug-susceptibility considerations.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Pulmonary Tuberculosis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Bronchiectasis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Massive hemoptysis (> 300 mL/24h).
management_principles: Respiratory isolation, notify public health, sputum AFB x3 on consecutive days, CXR, IGRA, HIV counselling and testing, contact tracing (4 household contacts + workplace), RIPE therapy if confirmed
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
Provide clear patient education, address patient concerns, and establish explicit follow-up and safety-netting instructions.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: coughing up blood twice this morning

two episodes of haemoptysis — approximately 2 tablespoons each time, bright red blood mixed with sputum, associated mild right-sided pleuritic chest pain, 3-week history of dry cough and fever, 4kg weight loss over 2 months, night sweats
reference_soap.objective: O2 saturation, CXR (apical shadowing, cavitation?), sputum AFB x3, Mantoux/IGRA, HIV test, FBC, CRP. ISOLATE pending results.
reference_soap.assessment: Pulmonary tuberculosis until proven otherwise. DDx: community acquired pneumonia, bronchiectasis, PE with pulmonary infarction, lung malignancy (less likely at 29).
reference_soap.plan: Assess airway, breathing, circulation, haemoptysis volume, and oxygenation urgently; seek emergency care for increasing bleeding, respiratory distress, hypoxemia, hemodynamic instability, or concerning chest pain. Use respiratory isolation and notify public health according to local protocol, obtain appropriate microbiologic testing and imaging, and arrange specialist-guided treatment and contact tracing once indicated.

learning_objectives: Elicit TB risk factors systematically: immigration, contacts, occupation, HIV status
Handle haemoptysis history sensitively in a frightened patient
Explain isolation and public health notification appropriately
Demonstrate cultural sensitivity with an immigrant patient

teaching.one_liner: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection causing chronic cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis.
red_flags: Severe hypoxemia, respiratory distress, or hemodynamic instability
Increasing bleeding, syncope, or pleuritic chest pain with PE or ACS concern

must_ask.say: How long have you had this cough, and are you coughing up blood streaks?
Do you wake up drenched in sweat at night or suffer from unexplained low-grade fevers?
Have you lost weight rapidly without trying over recent months?
Have you been around anyone diagnosed with active tuberculosis or lived in endemic regions?
Do you have medical conditions or take immunosuppressive medications that lower immunity?

history.answer: I started coughing up blood twice this morning, and it really terrified me.
It definitely came up when I was coughing; I did not throw up, and it was not dripping down the back of my throat.
It happened twice this morning, about two tablespoons each time.
It was bright red blood mixed together with some phlegm, not frothy pink or dark brown.
This morning was the very first time in my life that I have ever coughed up blood.
I have had a nagging dry cough for the past three weeks that gradually became worse.
No, I have never had chronic daily yellow phlegm or bad-smelling sputum, and I have never had repeated bouts of pneumonia.
I have felt warm and had a low fever on and off for the last three weeks, usually worse in the evenings.
Yes, I wake up drenched in sweat at night so badly that I have to change my clothes, and I have felt unusually tired.
I have lost about 4 kilograms over the past two months without trying to diet.
I feel a mild, sharp pain on the right side of my chest whenever I take a deep breath or cough, but I am not short of breath right now.
history.topic: Chest pain and shortness of breath

history.answer: No, neither leg is swollen, red, or painful.
I take birth control pills and took a flight when I moved here six months ago, but I have not had any surgery or been stuck in bed.
No, I can lie flat comfortably and I do not wake up gasping for air.
No nosebleeds, no crusting in my nose, and no facial or sinus pain.
My urine looks normal light yellow, never dark like tea or cola, and I make normal amounts.
No, I do not have bleeding gums, unexplained bruises, or skin spots, and I do not take blood thinners.
No nausea, no stomach pain, no vomiting, and my bowel movements are normal brown without any black tarry stools.
I do not have HIV, I do not take steroids or immune-suppressing drugs, and I do not have diabetes.
I wondered if I caught a severe lung bug during my plane flight six months ago.
I am terrified because I have never coughed blood before, and I worry it could be tuberculosis because my uncle had it back home.
I want to find out what is causing this bleeding right away and whether I need to stay away from other people.
I had mild asthma as a child, but I have no other chronic medical problems.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never stayed overnight in a hospital.
I take an oral contraceptive pill every day, and I have a salbutamol inhaler for asthma, but I rarely ever need to use it.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic cigarettes in my life.
I do not drink alcohol at all.
I work as an assistant in an outpatient medical clinic, and I share an apartment with four family members.
I moved here from the Philippines six months ago.
My uncle in the Philippines was diagnosed with and treated for tuberculosis two years ago, but my parents and siblings are healthy.
My last menstrual period was two weeks ago, my cycles are regular 28-day intervals on the pill, and there is no chance I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Alert, mildly anxious, speaking in full sentences without overt respiratory distress.
Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, pulse 84 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, body temperature 37.8°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Nasal mucosa pink without bleeding or crusting; pharynx clear with no blood pooling or active bleeding seen.
No palpable cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Jugular venous pulse is not elevated; carotid pulses are normal.
Chest expansion is symmetric without chest wall or rib tenderness.
Dullness to percussion over the right upper posterior and anterior chest; resonant over all other lung fields.
Tubular bronchial breath sounds and inspiratory crackles over the right upper lobe; clear breath sounds bilaterally in the lower zones.
Regular rhythm, normal S1 and S2, no heart murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Soft, non-tender throughout, non-distended, with normal bowel sounds.
No calf swelling, erythema, warmth, or tenderness bilaterally.
No peripheral edema in either lower extremity.
No digital clubbing, cyanosis, petechiae, or palmar erythema.
